interactions.summary: Jiang rejects easy crime-based distinctions between hell and purgatory and instead pressures the class toward an account centered on repentance, prayer, growth mindset, and the interior meaning of an apparently endless discipline.

claims.claim: Jiang states that the textual conditions for purgatory are repentance and the prayers of others rather than a simple crime taxonomy.
A student proposal Jiang takes seriously is that purgatorial suffering works because it is inhabited as an endless practice rather than as a finite task with a finish line.
Jiang explicitly frames this as a deep Dante question, implying that the decisive difference between hell and purgatory lies in the soul's orientation rather than the external punishment.
The Aristotelian golden mean analogy is acknowledged by Jiang as relevant but insufficient on its own to explain why the same apparent suffering can produce redemption in one case and not the other.

signature_moments.moment: The student answer Jiang favors makes salvation depend on doing the work without any calculable horizon of completion.
signature_moments.source_phrase: You can't do it as if there's a finish line
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns purgation into a present-tense disposition rather than a sentence to be served strategically.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang deliberately asks whether hell could simply be made into a long probationary purgatory and refuses the easy answer.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It forces the lecture toward its later free-will distinction.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture narrows its account of redemption away from legal categories and toward inner orientation, setting up the coming free-will formulation.

uncertainty_notes.note: The initial claim about deeds puncturing the fabric of society is exploratory and immediately treated as insufficient by Jiang, so it should not be lifted out as the lecture's settled criterion.
